stem: A stranger follows an employee through a badge door without badging. The employee holds the door because it feels polite. What is the event, and what should the employee do instead?
choices: Tailgating. The employee should refuse the courtesy and send the person to reception
Shoulder surfing, which is fixed by holding the door wider
A brute-force attack on the door pins
A distributed denial of service
explanation: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a door you did not unlock. Politeness is how it works. The employee should not grant access. They can be courteous and still send the person to reception to badge in. Shoulder surfing is watching a screen. Brute force is password guessing. A DDoS is a traffic flood.
choiceNotes: Tailgating is the unbadged follow-through. Reception, not the held door, is the right path.
Shoulder surfing is reading a screen or a keypad over someone's shoulder. It is not a door event.
Brute force tries many authentication values. It is not a person walking in behind you.
A DDoS overwhelms a service from many sources. It does not walk through a lobby door.

stem: A building entrance has two doors that never open at the same time, so a person badges through one and is held before the second opens. What is that entrance called in current CompTIA language?
choices: An access control vestibule
A honeypot
A proxy server
A full tunnel
explanation: An access control vestibule is the two-door entry that admits one party at a time. Older material called it a mantrap. It is a physical control against tailgating. A honeypot is a decoy system. A proxy fetches network traffic. A full tunnel is a VPN mode.
choiceNotes: The vestibule is the physical interlock. One door shuts before the other opens.
A honeypot is a decoy computer, not a lobby.
A proxy is a network service. It does not hold a person between two doors.
A full tunnel sends all VPN traffic to the company. It is not an entrance.

stem: A receptionist can see customer SSNs on a monitor that faces the waiting room. Which two controls reduce that exposure? (Choose two.)
choices: A privacy screen
Turning the monitor away from the waiting room
Posting the SSNs on the window
Disabling the screensaver lock
explanation: Shoulder surfing works because the screen faces the wrong people. A privacy filter narrows the angle, and turning the monitor removes the audience. Posting the numbers and disabling the lock make the exposure worse. This is physical and operational, not a firewall change.
choiceNotes: A privacy screen makes the off-angle view useless. It belongs on a monitor that strangers can see.
Aiming the monitor at the receptionist, not the lobby, removes the line of sight.
Posting SSNs is a disclosure. It is the incident, not the control.
A lock that never engages leaves the same data up when the receptionist walks away.

stem: A standard user is given local administrator rights on a shared kiosk 'so installs are easier.' Which principle did that break?
choices: Least privilege
The law of large numbers
Open addressing
Full-disk striping
explanation: Least privilege means each account gets only the access the job needs. A kiosk user who can install software can also disable controls and persist malware. Use a standard account, and elevate a technician account only for the install. Large numbers, open addressing, and striping are not access principles.
choiceNotes: Least privilege is the broken rule. Take the admin right back off the kiosk account.
The law of large numbers is statistics. It is not an access-control principle.
Open addressing is a programming idea, not a Windows rights model.
Striping is RAID 0. It does not describe who should be an administrator.

stem: A small office still uses WEP because 'it was the default.' Which replacement is acceptable, and which statement about WEP is true?
choices: Use WPA2-AES or WPA3. WEP is broken and should not be left in place
WEP is stronger than WPA3
TKIP is the modern cipher to add to WEP
Open authentication is safer than WPA2 because it needs no password
explanation: WEP can be broken quickly and does not belong on a current network. WPA2 with AES, or WPA3, is the replacement. TKIP is a legacy cipher from the original WPA era and is not the upgrade path. An open network removes authentication entirely.
choiceNotes: WPA2-AES or WPA3 replaces WEP. Do not leave the old default running.
WEP is the weak, retired option. WPA3 is far stronger.
TKIP is obsolete. Adding it to WEP does not create a modern network.
An open network lets anyone associate. It is not safer than WPA2.

stem: Employees each have a directory account. The office wants wireless that disables one person when they leave, without changing a password taped to the router. Which design is that?
choices: WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise with RADIUS
WPA2-Personal with the password on the router
WEP with a shared hex key
An open SSID with a hidden name
explanation: Enterprise Wi-Fi uses 802.1X and RADIUS so each person authenticates as themselves. Disabling the account removes that person. A personal passphrase is shared, so a departure means a new password for everyone. WEP and an open SSID are not account-based.
choiceNotes: Enterprise plus RADIUS is per-user. Disable the account and the passphrase on the wall stays out of the design.
A shared personal passphrase is the operational problem. It does not disable one person.
WEP is a broken shared key. It has no per-user disable.
An open network does not identify the employee, hidden name or not.

stem: A domain login fails with a clock-related error, and the PC's time is six minutes off from the domain controller. Which authentication system is famously sensitive to that skew?
choices: Kerberos
A cable tester
exFAT
A laser fuser
explanation: Kerberos tickets are time-stamped, and domain logons fail when the client and the domain controller drift too far, classically about five minutes. Fix the time service so the PC syncs to the domain. A cable tester, a file system, and a fuser do not issue tickets.
choiceNotes: Kerberos is the time-sensitive domain authentication. Correct the clock and the logon can proceed.
A cable tester checks wires. It does not care that a clock is six minutes off.
exFAT is a file system. It does not authenticate a domain user.
A fuser melts toner. It does not check Kerberos time.

stem: A user installed a free 'PDF converter' from a pop-up ad. The tool added a browser toolbar and a process that emails the user's keystrokes. The file they wanted never converted. What kind of malware arrived disguised as a useful program?
choices: A Trojan
A worm, because the user did not run anything
A boot-sector virus only, with no user action
A failed Windows update and nothing else
explanation: A Trojan pretends to be something useful so the user runs it. This converter was the disguise, and the toolbar and the keystroke theft are the payload. A worm spreads on its own. A boot-sector virus infects the boot area. A failed update does not install a toolbar from an ad.
choiceNotes: The Trojan is the fake tool. The user ran it, which is how a Trojan gets in.
A worm does not need the user to install a disguise. Here the user did install one.
A boot-sector infection is a different payload and a different location. The ad installer is a Trojan.
Windows Update did not ask the user to run a converter from a pop-up.

stem: A PC is loud, hot, and slow. Task Manager shows an unknown process using almost all of the CPU, and there is no ransom note. What malware class fits, and what is a reasonable first containment step?
choices: A cryptominer. Disconnect the PC from the network and identify the process before you replace the fan
A dead fan only, so ignore the process
A failed fuser
A healthy indexer that should be left at 100 percent forever
explanation: Cryptominers spend the CPU, and sometimes the GPU, to mine. The fan is loud because of the load, not necessarily because the fan failed. Isolate the PC so it stops talking to its controller, then follow the malware-removal process. Replacing the fan first ignores the process that is creating the heat.
choiceNotes: The unknown process at full CPU is the miner. Isolate first, then remove it. The fan may be innocent.
A dead fan is possible in other stories. This story hands you the process. Do not ignore it.
A fuser is in a printer. It does not peg a PC's CPU.
An indexer spikes and then settles. A permanent unknown 100 percent process is not healthy indexing.

stem: Passwords keep being stolen even after a reputable scan finds nothing. The technician finds a small device plugged between the USB keyboard and the PC. What is that device, and what should happen to it?
choices: A hardware keylogger. Remove it, then change passwords from a known-clean machine
A required Windows update dongle that should stay
A PoE injector for the keyboard
A loopback plug that improves typing
explanation: A hardware keylogger records keystrokes from the cable, so software scans of the disk never see it. Remove it, keep it as evidence if policy says so, and change the exposed passwords from a machine you trust. Do not type the new passwords on the same compromised keyboard path. It is not an update dongle, a PoE device, or a loopback plug.
choiceNotes: Remove the inline logger. Software could not see it because it never lived on the disk.
Windows updates do not arrive as a mystery device in the keyboard cable.
PoE powers network devices over Ethernet. A keyboard does not take PoE from a USB pigtail.
A loopback plug tests a network port. It does not sit on a keyboard cable.

stem: The finance director receives an email that looks like the chief executive, demanding an immediate wire transfer and telling them not to call. What is that targeted email?
choices: Whaling
A pop-up blocker test
A cable certification
A SMART failure
explanation: Whaling targets a high-value person, often with a business-email lookalike and urgency. The right move is to verify out of band, using a known phone number, and not to wire from the email. It is a form of phishing aimed up the org chart. A pop-up blocker, a cable certifier, and SMART are unrelated.
choiceNotes: Whaling is the executive-targeted fraud. Stop and verify using a channel you already trust.
A pop-up blocker is a browser feature. It did not send this wire request.
Cable certification tests wiring. It does not impersonate a CEO.
SMART reports disk health. It does not write emails.

stem: A caller says they are from 'Microsoft support,' quotes the user's name, and wants a remote-control tool installed now. The user did not open a ticket. What is the call, and what should the user do?
choices: Vishing. Hang up and call the company back on a published number if support was really expected
A normal patch window. Install the tool
An RFID test
A RAID rebuild
explanation: Vishing is phishing by voice. Unsolicited remote-control requests are a classic. The safe move is to hang up and use a number you look up yourself. Installing the tool gives a stranger the desktop. RFID and RAID are not phone scams.
choiceNotes: Hang up. If the company really needs access, they can be reached through a number you find, not one the caller pressures you to use.
An unexpected support call that demands software is not a patch window.
RFID reads badges and tags. It does not phone users.
A RAID rebuild is a disk operation. It does not ask for remote control.

stem: A login page stops accepting a password after five bad tries and locks the account for fifteen minutes. Which attack is that control slowing down?
choices: A brute-force or dictionary guessing attack
A tailgating event at the door
A swollen battery
A failed fuser
explanation: Brute force tries every combination. A dictionary tries likely words. A lockout makes both too slow to finish online, and it gives you an alert. It does not stop someone who already stole the password. Tailgating, a battery, and a fuser are physical problems of other kinds.
choiceNotes: Lockout is aimed at online guessing. Five fast failures are exactly the pattern it is there to interrupt.
Tailgating is a person behind another person at a door. A password lockout does not see the door.
A swollen battery is a hardware hazard. Account lockout does not describe it.
A fuser smears toner. It is not an authentication attack.

stem: A web form's symptom, described by the developer, is that typed input is being treated as part of a database command, and records changed. No exploit steps are needed to answer. Which threat is that?
choices: SQL injection
Shoulder surfing
A brownout
A stuck pixel
explanation: SQL injection is input that changes a database query because the application built the command out of the text the user typed. The fix is parameterized queries and validation, which is the developer's job. The help desk recognizes the name. Shoulder surfing is visual. A brownout is power. A stuck pixel is a display defect.
choiceNotes: The input became part of the database command. That is SQL injection, and the repair is in the application, not in a longer password.
Shoulder surfing watches a screen. It does not rewrite a query.
A brownout is a voltage sag. It does not change how a form talks to a database.
A stuck pixel is one dot on a panel. It does not edit records.

stem: A user wants one folder encrypted so that another local account cannot read it, without encrypting the entire drive. The PC is Windows 10 Pro. Which feature is the folder-level one?
choices: EFS
BitLocker on the whole volume, which is more than they asked for
exFAT encryption, which does not exist
A BIOS supervisor password, which encrypts folders
explanation: EFS encrypts files and folders for a user and is available on Pro. Another local account without the key cannot read the file. BitLocker encrypts the whole volume, which is the right tool for a stolen laptop and more than this request. exFAT does not offer EFS. A firmware password does not encrypt a folder.
choiceNotes: EFS is the per-file and per-folder encryption. It matches 'one folder' on Pro.
BitLocker is whole-volume encryption. It works, and it is a bigger control than the user asked for.
exFAT is a file system without EFS. Copying an EFS file to exFAT or FAT32 strips the encryption.
A firmware password gates setup or boot. It does not encrypt one folder.

stem: A laptop is lost at an airport. The disk was encrypted with BitLocker, and the key is in the company escrow. Which statement is the accurate reassurance?
choices: BitLocker protects the data at rest even if the thief moves the drive to another PC
BitLocker only helps while the laptop is on and unlocked
A BIOS password alone would have encrypted the disk the same way
EFS on one folder would have encrypted the shut-down operating system
explanation: BitLocker encrypts the volume. Pulled out and attached elsewhere, the drive still demands the key. That is data at rest. A firmware password without encryption does not stop someone who removes the disk. EFS protects selected files for a user and is not the same as encrypting the whole shut-down OS. The escrowed key is how the company recovers a returned laptop.
choiceNotes: The lost drive stays unreadable without the BitLocker key. That is the point of the full-disk encryption.
The protection matters most when the machine is off or the drive is moved. An unlocked running session is a different problem.
A BIOS password is not disk encryption. The thief can move an unencrypted disk.
EFS would not have encrypted the whole operating system volume. BitLocker did.

stem: A standard user double-clicks an installer and gets a credential prompt, not a simple yes/no. An administrator on the same PC gets a consent prompt. What is that prompt system?
choices: User Account Control
The print spooler
exFAT
A captive portal
explanation: UAC asks for elevation. A standard user must supply an administrator credential. An administrator confirms consent. That split is expected, not malware, when the user just launched an installer. An unexpected prompt when nobody launched anything should be cancelled. The spooler, exFAT, and a captive portal do not ask for elevation.
choiceNotes: UAC is the elevation prompt. The credential form is what a standard user should see.
The spooler prints. It does not ask for an administrator password to start an installer.
exFAT is a file system. It does not draw the consent dialog.
A captive portal is a network login page. It is not the local UAC prompt.

stem: A user copies an EFS-encrypted file to a FAT32 USB stick so they can open it at home on a PC that does not have their certificate. What happens to the encryption, and why?
choices: The copy on FAT32 is not EFS-encrypted, because FAT32 cannot store EFS
FAT32 keeps EFS and the home PC can open it with no key
The copy becomes BitLocker To Go automatically
EFS converts the file into a BitLocker volume
explanation: EFS depends on NTFS. Copying to FAT32, exFAT, or a share that does not support EFS writes a decrypted copy, as long as the user who has the key does the copy. The home PC can read it because it is no longer encrypted, which is also the data-loss risk. BitLocker To Go is a separate way to encrypt a removable drive, and it does not happen by itself.
choiceNotes: FAT32 drops EFS. The file on the stick is clear text. Use BitLocker To Go if the stick itself must be encrypted.
The home PC can open it only because the encryption did not survive the copy. That is not FAT32 'keeping' EFS.
Nothing automatically wraps the file in BitLocker To Go. That is a separate choice.
EFS does not turn a file into a BitLocker volume. They are different features.

stem: A front-desk PC is left signed in over lunch, and anyone in the lobby can use it. Which control locks it after a short idle without relying on the user to remember?
choices: A screensaver or sleep lock that requires a password
A shared generic login with no password
Disabling the lock screen
Writing the password on the monitor
explanation: An automatic lock after idle covers the lunch break the user will forget. The lobby PC should also be a standard account. A shared passwordless login, a disabled lock, and a password on the bezel are the failures the lock is there to replace.
choiceNotes: The idle lock does not depend on the receptionist remembering. Turn it on and require the password to resume.
A passwordless shared account is the exposure. It is not a control.
Disabling the lock screen leaves the session open, which is the current problem.
A password on the monitor publishes the credential to the lobby.

stem: A PC still has the Guest account enabled, AutoPlay on, and the local administrator named Administrator with a blank password. Which hardening set is appropriate?
choices: Disable Guest, disable AutoPlay and AutoRun, rename and password the administrator
Enable Guest for vendors and clear the administrator password
Turn AutoRun on so USB tools install themselves
Post the administrator password on the intranet homepage
explanation: Guest is an extra door. AutoRun and AutoPlay let inserted media do more than the user intended. The built-in Administrator name with no password is the first thing a guesser tries. Disable Guest, shut off the auto behaviors, and give the administrator a real password and preferably a less obvious name. Publishing the password undoes the work.
choiceNotes: That trio closes the obvious local doors. Do all three, not one.
Guest plus a blank administrator password is the insecure starting point, not the fix.
AutoRun launching USB programs is the behavior you are turning off.
An intranet post is a broadcast of the secret. It is not hardening.

stem: A technician sets a firmware supervisor password and leaves the disk unencrypted. A thief removes the drive and attaches it to another PC. What can the thief do, and what control was missing?
choices: Read the disk. BitLocker, not the firmware password, was the missing control
Nothing, because a firmware password encrypts the platters
Boot the original PC without any password, because supervisor passwords do not affect boot
The thief is stopped by exFAT
explanation: A supervisor password can stop someone from changing setup or booting that particular machine. It does not encrypt sectors. The drive in a second PC is just a drive. BitLocker is the control that still applies after the drive is moved. exFAT is only a file system.
choiceNotes: The firmware password stayed with the original motherboard. BitLocker would have stayed with the data.
Setup passwords do not scramble sectors. The second PC reads an unencrypted disk.
A supervisor password can restrict setup. The point of this theft is that the thief does not need to boot the original PC at all.
exFAT does not encrypt anything. It would not stop the second PC.

stem: A company phone is stolen on a commute. MDM is enrolled. What should happen first, according to a normal lost-device procedure?
choices: Report it and use MDM to lock or wipe it, per the company policy
Post the loss and the owner's password on social media so coworkers know
Wait a week to see if the phone comes back before telling anyone
Send a new phone with the same password and leave the old one enrolled and unlocked
explanation: Speed matters. MDM can lock, locate, or wipe company data. Policy says who may trigger that. Social media expands the disclosure. Waiting leaves mail and tokens exposed. A replacement that reuses the stolen password, and that leaves the old device trusted, continues the incident.
choiceNotes: Report and contain with MDM. The policy is what decides lock versus wipe.
Posting the password is a second incident. Do not do it.
A week is a long time for an unlocked mailbox to sit in a stranger's pocket.
Reuse of the password and trust of the stolen device keeps the thief enrolled.

stem: A user sideloads an APK that arrived in a text message. The app then shows ads in other apps and requests accessibility access. What is the risk, and what should the user do?
choices: The APK is an untrusted install. Remove it, scan, and do not grant accessibility to a texted app
Texted APKs are the official store and are always safe
Accessibility access cannot be abused
Ads in other apps prove the phone's battery is healthy
explanation: An APK from a text is an untrusted source. Accessibility permission lets a malicious app read and drive the screen, which is more power than a game needs. Uninstall it, run a scan, and change passwords that were typed afterward. The official store is not a text message. Ads bleeding into other apps are a malware symptom, not a battery report.
choiceNotes: Remove the sideloaded app and treat the text as hostile. Accessibility was the dangerous permission.
A text message is not the official store. Untrusted source is the whole point of the objective.
Accessibility can read the screen and click for the user. Malware asks for it on purpose.
Ad injection is a malware symptom. It says nothing good about the battery.

stem: A phone is jailbroken so a game can be installed from outside the vendor's controls. Company mail is on the same phone. Why does policy usually forbid the jailbreak?
choices: Jailbreak and root remove store protections and let unsigned code run with more privilege
Jailbreak enables full-disk encryption
Jailbreak is required for ordinary OS updates
A jailbroken phone cannot connect to any network, so it is safer
explanation: Jailbreak and root bypass the vendor's application controls. Code can run that the store would have rejected, and malware has an easier path to deep access. MDM should detect it and block company mail. It is not encryption, it is not how updates work, and the phone still connects to networks.
choiceNotes: The store model is the protection that jailbreak removes. Company data should not sit on that phone.
Jailbreak does not turn on encryption. It weakens the platform controls.
Updates come from the vendor. A jailbreak often blocks or delays them.
A jailbroken phone networks just fine. That is part of the risk, not a safety feature.

stem: A spinning hard drive from a leased PC must be disposed of so the previous tenant's data cannot be recovered. Degaussing is available. A stack of SSDs is next to it. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Degaussing can destroy the magnetic drive. It is not a reliable wipe for the SSDs
Degaussing is the preferred wipe for every SSD
A quick format is enough for the spinning drive
Throwing both in the trash meets a certificate-of-destruction requirement
explanation: Degaussing scrambles magnetic media. An SSD does not store data that way, so a degausser is the wrong tool and can leave the data recoverable. SSDs want a vendor secure-erase or physical destruction. A quick format only removes pointers. A trash can is not a certificate of destruction. If a vendor does the destruction, get the certificate.
choiceNotes: Degauss the magnetic disk if that is your method, and use a different, SSD-appropriate destruction for the flash.
SSDs are not reliably erased by a degausser. Do not put them in the same pile and assume they are clean.
A quick format leaves the data for recovery software. It is not disposal.
Trash is not destruction, and it produces no certificate.

stem: A drive is formatted with the normal Windows format and then given to another department. The giver says the old files are gone. What is wrong with that claim?
choices: A standard format removes the pointers and leaves the data recoverable. It is not a secure wipe
A standard format overwrites every sector several times by definition
Format physically shreds the platters
Format is stronger than incineration
explanation: A standard format rebuilds the file system. The old bytes are usually still on the media until something overwrites them. Recovery tools exist for this. A secure wipe or physical destruction is what disposal requires. Format does not shred platters, and it is not stronger than incineration.
choiceNotes: The pointers are gone and the data is not. Treat a formatted drive as still sensitive.
Multiple overwrite passes are a wiping procedure, not the default quick or standard format.
Format is a software action. The platters are intact.
Incineration destroys media. A format does not outrank it.

stem: A new SOHO router still answers to admin/admin. It has not been connected to the modem yet. What is the first configuration change?
choices: Change the default administrator password before it faces the internet
Enable WPS because the PIN is short and convenient
Leave the password and hide the SSID, which replaces the password
Forward every port to a PC
explanation: Default passwords are published. Change the administrator password before the router is reachable. WPS PINs are brute-forceable and should be off. Hiding the SSID is not authentication. Forwarding every port exposes every service. Firmware updates come right after the password.
choiceNotes: The default password is the first door to close. Do it before the WAN is attached.
WPS is a weakness. Convenience of a short PIN is exactly why it gets guessed.
A hidden name is not a password. Anyone who sees a client can learn the name.
Forwarding every port is the opposite of a hardened SOHO router.

stem: A SOHO router has UPnP enabled, and a game console has opened several inbound ports the owner did not intend to publish. What is the cautious change?
choices: Disable UPnP and remove the port forwards that are not required
Enable UPnP on the WAN side as well
Set the firewall to allow all
Put the console in the screened subnet and call that private
explanation: UPnP lets devices punch inbound holes without a person approving them. Turn it off unless you have a specific need, and delete the forwards you did not ask for. A screened subnet or DMZ host on a home router exposes a machine. It is not a privacy feature. Allow-all is not a firewall policy.
choiceNotes: UPnP created the holes. Disable it and close the forwards you do not need.
More UPnP means more unsolicited holes. That is the wrong direction.
Allow-all removes the firewall. It does not correct a surprise forward.
The home 'DMZ host' is an exposed host. It is not where you hide a console.

stem: A technician hides the SSID, leaves WPA2-Personal with a password of 'password,' and tells the owner the network is now secure because the name is invisible. What is the accurate correction?
choices: Hiding the SSID is not access control. The weak passphrase is the problem to fix, preferably with WPA3 or a long passphrase
A hidden SSID cannot be seen by any client or tool
The password 'password' is strong because the SSID is hidden
WEP would be stronger in this design
explanation: Clients and simple scanners still reveal a hidden SSID. The passphrase is the actual secret, and 'password' is not one. Use a long unique passphrase or WPA3-Personal, and do not describe hiding the name as the security. WEP would make it worse.
choiceNotes: Fix the passphrase and the protocol. The hidden name is not the control you should be selling.
Hidden does not mean undetectable. Association traffic still carries the name.
A terrible passphrase stays terrible when the name is hidden.
WEP is weaker than WPA2. It is not the upgrade.

stem: A browser warns that a bank's certificate is not trusted and the name does not match. The user is on cafe Wi-Fi. What should they do?
choices: Stop. Do not enter the password. Leave the page and use a trusted network or the bank's app
Click through, because banks always have certificate warnings
Disable certificate checking permanently
Install the certificate the page offers so the warning goes away
explanation: A name mismatch or an untrusted issuer on a bank is a reason to stop. It can be an interception, a lookalike site, or a clock problem. You do not install a certificate a stranger's page offers, and you do not turn checking off. If the PC clock is wildly wrong, that is a separate, checkable cause. On cafe Wi-Fi, assume the warning matters.
choiceNotes: Stop. The warning is the browser doing its job. Use a path you trust instead of clicking through.
Banks do not normally throw certificate errors. Treating them as normal trains people to ignore real ones.
Disabling the check removes the protection for every later site.
Installing a prompted certificate teaches the browser to trust the interceptor.

stem: A user believes private-browsing mode hides them from their company proxy and from the websites they visit. What does private mode actually limit?
choices: Local history, cookies, and the local record of the session. The network can still see the traffic
It encrypts traffic even on HTTP and hides the destination from the proxy
It disables the company firewall
It makes the PC's MAC address random on every packet
explanation: Private mode keeps the session out of the local profile. It does not change what the proxy, the ISP, or the website can see, and it does not turn HTTP into HTTPS. The firewall still applies. MAC randomization, where it exists, is a different feature and is not 'every packet.'
choiceNotes: Private mode is a local-history control. Explain that the company network still sees the visit.
HTTP stays HTTP. A proxy still sees the destination of plain traffic and the name of HTTPS sites in many designs.
The firewall does not care which browser mode you picked.
Private mode is not a per-packet MAC change. Do not describe it as anonymity.
